title: Review: Experimental methods and practical skills; Uncertainties and errors
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: MS06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MS06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MS02-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; MS02-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: MS02-1#N.5, MS06-1#N.7, MS02-1#N.11, MS06-1#N.4, MS02-1#N.8, MS06-1#N.13, MS02-1#N.3, MS06-1#N.12. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Control variables
items.clue: Everything else that could affect the result, kept fixed.

items.label: Independent variable
items.clue: The one quantity you deliberately change in an experiment.

items.label: Resolution
items.clue: Smallest change an instrument can show, such as 1 mm on a rule.

items.label: Anomaly
items.clue: Result far from the pattern, to be checked, repeated or left out of the mean.

questions.stem: A ball's fall is timed four times: 0.62 s, 0.57 s, 0.65 s, 0.60 s. The stopwatch reads to 0.01 s. Which is the best way to write the result?
questions.explanation: Mean = 2.44 ÷ 4 = 0.61 s. Half the range = (0.65 − 0.57) ÷ 2 = 0.04 s. The scatter is far bigger than the resolution, so it sets the uncertainty.

questions.stem: One complete cycle of a wave on an oscilloscope screen spans 2.5 divisions. The time-base is set to 2.0 ms div⁻¹. What is the frequency of the signal?

options.text: 200 Hz
5.0 Hz

questions.stem: A student measures the diameter of a wire five times with a micrometer: 0.55, 0.56, 0.55, 0.55, 0.56 mm. Later she notices that the micrometer reads 0.03 mm when fully closed. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The readings are accurate, because they agree closely with each other.
Taking more readings and averaging them would remove the error.
The readings are precise but not accurate; subtract 0.03 mm from each.
The error is random, so a micrometer with a finer resolution is needed.

questions.explanation: Small spread means precise. The zero error is systematic: correct it by subtracting the zero reading, giving about 0.52–0.53 mm.

questions.stem: On a pair of vernier callipers, the vernier's zero lies between the 31 mm and 32 mm marks of the main scale. Vernier mark 6 lines up exactly with a main-scale mark. What is the reading?

options.text: 37 mm

questions.explanation: Main scale up to the vernier's zero: 31 mm. Vernier mark 6 lines up: 6 × 0.1 mm = 0.6 mm. Reading = 31.6 mm.

questions.stem: The resistivity of a wire is ρ = RA/L, where A = πd²/4. The percentage uncertainties are: R 3.0%, d 1.0%, L 0.5%. What is the percentage uncertainty in ρ?
questions.explanation: 3.0% + 2 × 1.0% + 0.5% = 5.5%. Dividing by L still adds its percentage uncertainty; π and 4 add none.

questions.stem: A student has a ruler with 1 mm divisions and wants the thickness of one sheet of paper, about 0.1 mm. Which choice and reason are both correct?

options.text: Measure one sheet ten times and average, because averaging reduces the uncertainty.
Measure a stack of 200 sheets and divide by 200, because the reading uncertainty is shared out.
Measure a stack of 10 sheets ten times and average, because more readings always help.
Measure a stack of 200 sheets and divide by 200, because any calibration error in the ruler then cancels.

questions.stem: A student times a trolley rolling down a ramp with a hand-held stopwatch that reads to 0.01 s. Her five times vary by about 0.2 s. Which change would most reduce the effect of this random error on her result?

options.text: Use a stopwatch that reads to 0.001 s instead of 0.01 s.
Check that the stopwatch reads zero before each timing.
Subtract her typical reaction time from each reading.
Time the run with light gates and an electronic timer.

questions.explanation: The varying human reaction is the source of the scatter. Automatic timing removes it.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the time t for a ball to fall from rest depends on the drop height h. (h = ½gt², with g constant.) Which plan is best?

options.text: Drop the ball once from each of three heights, timing by hand; plot t against h.
Drop the ball three times from each of six heights, timing electronically; plot h against t.
Drop the ball three times from each of six heights, timing electronically; plot h against t².
Drop a ball three times from each of six heights, timing electronically, with a heavier ball for the greater heights.

questions.explanation: Enough values, repeats, no reaction time, and h = (g/2)t² gives a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.
